content: Inhaled budesonide is available in various doses for the treatment of chronic asthma. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of budesonide at different doses to determine whether a clinically significant dose-response relationship exists. A systematic search was conducted to identify controlled clinical trials, and randomized trials comparing different doses of budesonide in children and adults with chronic asthma were included. Two reviewers independently assessed the studies for inclusion and methodological quality. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer, and missing information was clarified by contacting the study authors. Quantitative analyses were conducted using specialized statistical software. A total of 24 studies, involving 3,907 participants, met the inclusion criteria. In patients with mild to moderately severe asthma who were not receiving oral steroids, no clinically meaningful differences were observed in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), morning peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR), symptom scores, or the use of rescue beta-2 agonists across a dose range of 200 to 1600 micrograms per day. However, in patients with moderate to severe asthma, treatment with 800 micrograms per day of budesonide significantly reduced the likelihood of withdrawal from trials due to asthma exacerbations compared to 200 micrograms per day. The relative risk for this outcome was 3.93 (95% confidence interval: 1.4 to 10.9), and this result was heavily influenced by a single large, high-quality randomized controlled trial (RCT). In patients with severe asthma, high-dose budesonide (1600 micrograms per day) demonstrated significant improvements in FEV1 compared to low-dose budesonide (200 micrograms per day). However, no significant differences were observed in morning PEFR. These findings were based on two large, high-quality RCTs. In patients with asthma who were being treated with oral steroids, no dose-dependent oral steroid-sparing effect was observed when comparing 1600 micrograms per day of budesonide to 800 or 400 micrograms per day. However, statistically significant, dose-dependent suppression of 24-hour urinary free cortisol excretion and serum cortisol levels following synthetic ACTH infusion was observed across a dose range of 800 to 3200 micrograms per day. The clinical significance of these changes in hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis function remains unclear. In conclusion, budesonide demonstrates a significant dose-response effect between low and high doses for improving FEV1 in severe asthma and reducing exacerbations in moderate to severe asthma. However, no significant dose-dependent improvements in FEV1, PEFR, or symptoms were observed in patients with mild to moderate asthma who were not receiving oral steroids. While dose-dependent alterations in sensitive measures of HPA axis function were evident, the clinical relevance of these findings is uncertain.
